concepts.name: Liquid asset and liability management
concepts.definition: Liquidity and return are inversely related: liquid assets earn less, and callable liabilities cost less but carry more withdrawal risk. A DI balances low-yield liquid assets against higher-yield illiquid assets, and low-cost, high-withdrawal-risk liabilities against costlier stable funding.
misconceptions: Thinking demand deposits are free to a bank

questions.prompt: Why is managing liquidity difficult for a bank?
options: Liquidity and return are inversely related: liquid assets earn less, and callable liabilities are cheaper but riskier
Liquid assets always earn the highest returns
Stable liabilities are the cheapest funding
Liquidity has no effect on profit
questions.explanation: More liquid assets have lower returns; more callable liabilities have lower costs but higher withdrawal risk.

questions.prompt: What makes an asset liquid, according to the lecture?
options: It trades in a deep market where even large volumes don't move the price
It pays a high interest rate
questions.explanation: Treasury notes and bonds are examples; the trade-off is a lower interest rate.
feedback: Long maturity usually means less liquid.

questions.prompt: What are the characteristics of demand deposits as a funding source?
options: High withdrawal risk and low cost
Low withdrawal risk and high cost
The most expensive funding a bank has
questions.explanation: Cheap but callable. Even with zero explicit interest they aren't free: banks bear processing costs.
feedback: That's stable funding like term deposits.
They can be withdrawn on demand.

questions.prompt: Interest rates on purchased funds in the short-term money market rise. What happens to a DI's desired liquid asset ratio?
questions.explanation: Borrowing to cover liquidity needs becomes costlier, so holding more liquid assets becomes relatively attractive.
feedback: Costlier borrowing makes stored liquidity more attractive, not less.
The lecture lists this as a determinant.

questions.prompt: Why are repos usually a cheaper source of funds than interbank loans?
options: Repos are collateralised, so lenders accept a lower yield
Repos have no rollover risk at all
questions.explanation: Interbank funds are unsecured and face rollover risk when lenders pull back.
feedback: The collateral, not a guarantee, makes them cheaper.
They're short-term and must be rolled over.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT a determinant of a DI's optimal liquid asset ratio listed in the lecture?
options: The size of the bank's branch network
The variability of deposit inflows and outflows
The liquidation costs of highly non-liquid assets
questions.explanation: The lecture also lists the interest rate on purchased funds or RBA liquidity facilities.

questions.prompt: The RBA does a buy-side repo with Bank A, crediting its Exchange Settlement account with $80m. What happens to the cash rate?
options: It tends to fall: more ES balances means banks need to borrow less overnight
It rises, because liquidity is drained
No effect: repos don't affect ES balances
It rises to the repo rate automatically
questions.explanation: The RBA manages ES supply to keep the cash rate near its target.

questions.prompt: The RBA does a 7-day repo with Bank A for $80m at 3.00% p.a. (actual/365). What does Bank A pay to unwind it?
A 14-day repo for $50m at 2.50% p.a. (actual/365). What's the repurchase price?

A depositor keeps $1,000 for six months and below $500 for the rest of the year. The account pays 4% p.a. on balances of $500 or more. They make 40 transactions a month, paying 5 cents each, which cost the bank 20 cents each. What is their gross interest return?
feedback: That uses the full 20-cent cost without netting the fee.

concepts.name: Deposit insurance, bank runs and moral hazard
concepts.definition: First-come, first-served deposits give depositors a reason to run, which can push a sound DI into failure. Deposit insurance (e.g. FDIC, up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category) removes the incentive to run, but flat premiums create moral hazard and reduce market discipline.
misconceptions: Thinking deposit insurance has no downside

questions.prompt: Why does deposit insurance stop bank runs?
options: If depositors believe their claim is completely secure, they have no incentive to run even if the bank is in trouble
It makes banks hold more cash
It bans withdrawals during a crisis
questions.explanation: The run incentive comes from first-come, first-served payment; insurance removes the fear of being last in line.

questions.prompt: Up to what amount does FDIC insurance cover depositors?
options: At least $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category
questions.explanation: It covers principal plus accrued interest up to the date of default.
feedback: That was Australia's original FCS cap.

questions.prompt: What is the moral hazard problem with deposit insurance?
options: Insured depositors stop monitoring banks and flat premiums don't charge for risk, so banks are encouraged to take more risk
Insurance makes deposits more expensive for depositors
questions.explanation: The lecture describes a trade-off between bank run risk and moral hazard risk.

questions.prompt: Deposit insurance premiums are flat, not linked to risk. What happens to banks' incentive to take risky investments?
questions.explanation: Risky banks pay the same as safe ones, so the cost of extra risk isn't charged: risk-taking rises.

questions.prompt: Apart from economic conditions, what's the second 'school of thought' on why the FDIC became insolvent at times?
options: Moral hazard: insurance reduced market discipline and premiums weren't linked to risk
Banks held too many Treasury securities
questions.explanation: The first school blames the environment (rate rises, collapsing oil, real estate and commodity prices; the housing collapse).
feedback: Rate rises were part of the first school.

questions.prompt: What does the FDIC chart of bank failures show?
options: Failures spike in crises: the 1930s, the late 1980s and around 2008–2010
Failures have never exceeded 50 in a year
questions.explanation: The late-1980s savings and loan crisis peaked near 280 failures a year.
feedback: The late-1980s peak was much higher.

questions.prompt: A sound bank faces a large, unexpected depositor drain with no deposit insurance. Trace what can happen.
options: Depositors queue because pay-outs are first come, first served; the bank fire-sells assets; losses can push it into insolvency
The bank simply borrows from depositors
Nothing, because sound banks can't fail
The regulator guarantees all deposits automatically
questions.explanation: The incentive to run first creates instability that deposit insurance is designed to remove.
feedback: Sound banks can be pushed into failure.

questions.prompt: Under the 1997 FDIC fee structure, which bank paid nothing for deposit insurance?
options: A well-capitalised bank in the healthy supervisory group
An undercapitalised bank of substantial supervisory concern
An adequately capitalised bank of supervisory concern
questions.explanation: Well-capitalised and healthy paid 0 cents per $100; undercapitalised with substantial concern paid 27 cents.
feedback: That bank paid the most (27 cents).
That was the 1993 flat-ish starting point.

concepts.name: Controlling DI risk taking
concepts.definition: Moral hazard can be reduced through stockholder discipline (risk-based premiums, higher capital, stricter closure rules), depositor discipline (insurance caps, insured depositor transfers) and regulator discipline (more thorough examinations, prompt corrective action).
misconceptions: Thinking an insurance cap can't be bypassed

questions.prompt: Which three types of discipline can mitigate deposit insurance moral hazard?
options: Central bank, treasury and court discipline
questions.explanation: The lecture works through each in turn.

questions.prompt: In the risk-based premium chart, Bank A is riskier than Bank B. What changes when premiums switch from flat to risk-based?
options: Bank A pays more and Bank B pays less than the flat $0.23 per $100
questions.explanation: A risk-based schedule rises with risk, so the risky bank pays more.
feedback: B is safer, so it pays less.

questions.prompt: What does an 'insured depositor transfer' do when a DI fails?
options: Moves insured deposits in full to another DI while uninsured depositors take a haircut
Transfers the bank's shares to depositors
questions.explanation: The haircut gives uninsured depositors a reason to monitor the bank.

questions.prompt: Regulators raise capital requirements. What happens to stockholders' stake in the bank's risky investments?
questions.explanation: Shareholders have more to lose, so they have more reason to restrain risk-taking.
feedback: More capital means more at stake.

questions.prompt: How can depositors get around an insurance cap?
options: By changing how deposits are structured and spreading them across institutions
By depositing more in one bank
questions.explanation: That weakens the depositor discipline the cap is meant to create.
feedback: That puts more above the cap.
The lecture says they can be bypassed.

questions.prompt: Why does 'too big to fail' weaken depositor discipline?
options: Depositors expect large banks to be rescued, giving them implicit coverage without a cap
Big banks pay higher deposit rates
questions.explanation: If depositors believe they'll be protected regardless, they don't monitor risk.

questions.prompt: Under the stricter closure rules described, when is a bank placed into receivership?
options: Within 90 days of its capital falling below 2% of assets (book value)
When it misses one interest payment
questions.explanation: Five capital zones bring progressively harsher mandatory actions as capital falls.

questions.prompt: A regulator wants to reduce moral hazard without making depositors run. Which mix fits the lecture best?
options: Risk-based premiums plus prompt corrective action, keeping insurance for small depositors
questions.explanation: Prices risk (stockholder discipline) and acts early (regulator discipline) while preserving run protection.

questions.prompt: Which factors does the lecture list as inputs to risk-based deposit insurance premiums?
options: Categories and concentrations of assets and liabilities, other factors affecting probability of loss, and the insurer's revenue needs
The number of branches and staff
questions.explanation: These factors link the premium to the risk each bank imposes on the fund.

concepts.name: The discount window (lender of last resort)
concepts.definition: A central bank facility lending short-term against high-quality collateral at the discount rate. Primary credit for sound DIs (overnight, above the fed funds rate, any purpose); secondary credit for others at a higher rate, not to fund asset expansion.
misconceptions: Thinking secondary credit can fund growth

questions.prompt: What does a DI usually need to borrow from the discount window?
options: High-quality liquid assets to pledge as collateral
questions.explanation: The rate charged is the discount rate.

questions.prompt: Who can use primary credit?
questions.explanation: It's very short-term (typically overnight), priced above the fed funds rate, and can be used for any purpose.

questions.prompt: How does secondary credit differ from primary credit?
options: It's for DIs that don't qualify for primary credit, costs more, and can't fund an expansion of the borrower's assets
It's cheaper and has no conditions
It's only for the largest banks
questions.explanation: It's temporary: a bridge back to market funding or an orderly resolution.
feedback: It costs more and has conditions.

questions.prompt: A DI moves from primary to secondary discount window credit. What happens to its borrowing rate?
questions.explanation: Secondary credit is priced above the primary credit rate.

questions.prompt: A troubled DI wants discount window funds to grow its loan book quickly. What does the lecture suggest?
options: It can't: secondary credit may not be used to fund an expansion of the borrower's assets
It can, at the primary credit rate
It can, if it's too big to fail
questions.explanation: Secondary credit should lead back to market funding or an orderly resolution.
feedback: A troubled DI wouldn't qualify for primary credit.
Not a rule in the lecture.

concepts.name: Australia's deposit and wholesale funding guarantees
concepts.definition: Before October 2008, Australia (with New Zealand) was one of only two OECD countries without explicit deposit insurance, relying on APRA regulation and depositor preference. In 2008 it introduced the Financial Claims Scheme (free, deposits up to A$1m, cut to A$250,000 from February 2012) and the fee-based Wholesale Funding Guarantee.
misconceptions: Mixing up which scheme charged a fee

questions.prompt: Before October 2008, how did Australia protect depositors?
options: Through APRA regulation and depositor preference, without explicit deposit insurance
questions.explanation: Deposit insurance was viewed as expensive and incentive-perverting.

questions.prompt: What is the current cap under Australia's Financial Claims Scheme?
questions.explanation: It started at A$1 million in 2008 and was reduced in 2012.

questions.prompt: How did the Financial Claims Scheme and the Wholesale Funding Guarantee differ?
options: The FCS guaranteed deposits automatically at no cost; the WGS let eligible ADIs pay a risk-based fee to guarantee large deposits and wholesale funding
Both charged the same flat fee
The FCS covered only wholesale funding
questions.explanation: The WGS covered deposits above A$1 million and wholesale debt funding.
feedback: The WGS fee was risk-based; the FCS was free.

questions.prompt: Why did Australia introduce guarantees in 2008?
options: Other countries strengthened their deposit insurance and guarantees during the GFC, so Australian banks needed similar support to stay competitive
questions.explanation: Without matching support, funds could flow to guaranteed banks abroad.

questions.prompt: A depositor has A$400,000 in one Australian ADI that fails today. How much is guaranteed under the FCS?
questions.explanation: The cap has been A$250,000 since February 2012.
